system:
You are a computational cancer biologist searching CRISPR screen data for selective genetic dependencies: genes that cancer cells with a particular alteration (the biomarker) need more than other cancer cells do. Such genes are candidate drug targets with a built-in patient-selection strategy.

Work like a careful scientist:
1. Plan first with write_plan, and revise it as you learn.
2. Survey the data (genome_wide_top, scan_biomarker, scan_target) to generate candidate hypotheses.
3. Be sceptical before you believe a signal. Use inspect_association to check whether it is driven by one lineage or a disease subtype hiding inside a lineage, and whether the effect is large enough to matter. Ask whether the biology makes sense (paralog buffering, pathway dependence, oncogene addiction). A broadly essential target may lack a therapeutic window.
4. Check the literature with search_pubmed before registering, and judge novelty honestly.
5. Register only your best hypotheses (register_hypothesis). Registration is final and must come before replication. You have 5 replications, each of which must pass one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad cell lines and independent Sanger screens.
6. Report honestly with submit_findings. A hypothesis is replicated only if replicate() said so. Negative results are results. Never let what you remember from the literature override what the data show.

You have at most 30 model turns. Batch independent tool calls in one turn.
task_prompt:
Mission: Search freely for the most promising selective dependencies in the data.

Goal: identify up to 5 candidate selective dependencies, and favour candidates that are NOT already well established in the literature, since rediscovering textbook biology is not the aim. Pre-register, replicate, and submit honest findings, including failures.

input.mechanism: Paralogous V-ATPase V0 subunit a isoforms (a1 ubiquitous, a2 Golgi/lysosome). When a1 expression is lost, cells rely on a2 for proton-pump function; knockout of a2 becomes lethal. Paralog buffering gives a selective dependency in a1-low lines.

Paralogous V-ATPase proteolipid c-subunit isoforms (ATP6V0E1 and ATP6V0E2). Loss of E2 expression makes E1 the sole c-ring isoform; E1 knockout then becomes lethal due to loss of V-ATPase proton translocation.

SPAK (STK39) and OSR1 (OXSR1) are paralogous Ste20-family kinases that phosphorylate NKCC/KCC cotransporters for cell volume and ion homeostasis. Loss of SPAK leaves OSR1 as the sole effector, so OSR1 knockout becomes selectively lethal.

content.thinking:
Two of the three hypotheses held up, and H1 only partly, since Sanger had no altered lines to test it against. With two budget units left, I'm weighing whether to test one more candidate, perhaps LOSS_CRY1 against BCL6.

I'm leaning toward not registering LOSS_CRY1 against BCL6, since that lymphoma-specific result would be confounded by lineage and tell me less. I'll stop here and submit.

findings.claim: Lines with LOSS of ATP6V0E2 (a V-ATPase c-ring paralog) depend selectively on ATP6V0E1; the effect replicated in held-out Broad lines (p=1.2e-29) and independent Sanger screens (p=8e-26), with 23 discovery lines altered across esophagogastric, head and neck and other lineages, so it is not a single-lineage artifact.

LOSS of ATP6V0A1 predicts dependency on ATP6V0A2 in discovery lines (t=-15.8, driven partly by lymphoid lines but holds within lineage). It passed in held-out Broad lines (p=3e-12) but could not be tested in Sanger (zero altered lines), so it does not meet the replication criterion.

LOSS of STK39 (SPAK) predicts dependency on OXSR1 (OSR1) in discovery lines (t=-12.3, mostly lymphoid plus breast/uterus), and it passed in held-out Broad lines (p=6e-35). Sanger testing was not possible (only 2 altered lines), so the result is unconfirmed; the SPAK/OSR1 redundancy idea has some prior literature on ion transport.

input.summary: I surveyed the genome-wide biomarker-dependency pairs. Many of the strongest hits were lineage-restricted (e.g., B-cell lymphoma) or likely copy-number passenger effects (e.g., LOSS_RPP25 -> RPP25L), so I prioritized paralog-buffering hypotheses that are pan-lineage and biologically interpretable. Three were registered and tested. H2 (LOSS_ATP6V0E2 -> ATP6V0E1) replicated in both held-out Broad lines and independent Sanger screens. H1 (LOSS_ATP6V0A1 -> ATP6V0A2) and H3 (LOSS_STK39 -> OXSR1) passed the held-out Broad test, but the Sanger screen had too few altered lines to test, so they are not replicated under the stated criteria. Literature searches returned very few hits (the PubMed tool returned zero for many queries), so novelty calls are tentative. I did not register the other candidates (e.g., LOSS_CRY1 -> BCL6, LOSS_ACSL4 -> FOXA1), which looked more lineage-confounded on inspection (FOXA1 signal largely disappears outside breast). Two replication credits remain unused.
